findings.question: q-biology-human-body-control-movement-and-defense-0003
findings.quote: A muscle makes force only by shortening, so it can pull but not push.
findings.problem: The word "only" makes this false. A biceps muscle produces force while holding a weight still (an isometric contraction) and while slowly lowering it as the muscle lengthens (an eccentric contraction). Pulling does not require shortening. The related wrong-choice note also treats shortening versus lengthening as the test for force production.
findings.fix: Say that muscles exert pulling force, so opposing muscles move the forearm in opposite directions. Revise the note to check pulling versus pushing.

findings.question: q-biology-human-body-control-movement-and-defense-0004
findings.quote: Motor neurons carry signals away from them, to muscles and glands.
findings.problem: This explains the motor-neuron distractor instead of explaining only the correct answer. For example, it gives the function of the listed wrong choice "Motor neurons."
findings.fix: Keep only the sensory-neuron explanation; leave the motor-neuron comparison in its note.

findings.question: q-biology-human-body-control-movement-and-defense-0008
findings.quote: They belong to innate immunity, which builds no memory.
findings.problem: This is a false absolute. Innate immune cells can develop trained immunity; for example, BCG vaccination can produce lasting changes in monocytes and macrophages that strengthen later responses. This differs from antigen-specific memory B and T cells, but it contradicts "no memory."
findings.fix: Explain that the vaccine mechanism tested here is antigen-specific memory in B and T cells, rather than claiming innate immunity has no memory of any kind.

findings.question: q-biology-human-body-control-movement-and-defense-0008
findings.quote: Each antibody binds one particular antigen.
findings.problem: This overstates specificity. An antibody recognizes an epitope and can cross-react with similar epitopes on different antigens; for example, an antibody can bind related proteins from different viral strains. Specificity does not mean exactly one antigen.
findings.fix: Say that antibodies recognize particular targets and do not match every antigen.
